Abstract: The development of agentic software engineering (ASE) is shifting the software development process, specifically by adopting autonomous agents into the fundamental software development process, where autonomous agents using large language models (LLMs) and artificial intelligence (AI) make decisions, write code, and collaborate across the entire software development lifecycle. The systematic review is a summary of literature on the agentic software engineering methodologies, frameworks, and techniques published in 2022-2025. We identify and compare methods based on autonomous coding, multi-agent systems, iterative refinement, and human-agent collaboration, drawing on 61 high-quality studies. We find that LLM-based agents show substantial potential in automated software engineering and that recent work is exploring new trends in agent cooperation, reasoning systems, and tool integration. We recognize such key challenges as the coordination procedures, reliability, explainability, and the ethical issues. This review characterizes the emerging role of agentic software engineering in improving the productivity of developers, the quality of their code, and the automation of their processes, and it offers a structured roadmap for future research. With the rapid evolution of the field, agentic approaches will tend to transform the conception, creation, and maintenance of software and provide more autonomous, adaptive, and intelligent systems.

Abstract: Autonomous agent systems powered by Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated promising capabilities in automating complex tasks. However, current evaluations largely rely on success rates without systematically analyzing the interactions, communication mechanisms, and failure causes within these systems. To bridge this gap, we present a benchmark of 34 representative programmable tasks designed to rigorously assess autonomous agents. Abstract: Software practitioners increasingly use AI coding agents that generate test code alongside production code in open-source pull requests (PRs). Recent studies report more than 932,000 agent-authored PRs across more than 116,000 repositories, yet whether their test files contain meaningful verification logic remains underexplored. Test files lacking explicit assertions execute code without verifying behavior, so quality gates based on test-file presence overestimate verification strength. The goal of this paper is to help practitioners assess the verification strength of agent-authored patches by characterizing oracle signals and their link to merge outcomes and review effort. Abstract: Cloud platforms have made quantum hardware accessible for research, while autonomous agents powered by large language models are increasingly used to generate code. When such an agent receives a computational problem, however, it often cannot determine whether quantum computing offers a real benefit or whether the problem is better suited to classical hardware. To address this gap, this article proposes a three-stage decision framework. The first stage extracts structural features from the problem description: problem type, search space size, and the presence of a verification oracle. The second stage assigns a quantum advantage classification from established properties of algorithms suited to noisy intermediate-scale quantum devices. The third stage verifies whether the resulting circuit can be executed on real hardware. Circuit generation is implemented for Grover’s search, the quantum approximate optimization algorithm, and the variational quantum eigensolver, and evaluated on a simulator under six noise channels. An ablation study compares three classifiers on a benchmark of 15 standard and 12 adversarial descriptions: the deterministic framework, a feedforward network trained by back-propagation, and a standalone language model. Their aggregate accuracy is within sampling variation, yet they fail on categorically different problems, and the learned classifier never succeeds where reasoning about problem scale is required. The feasibility gate is further validated against circuits compiled for the coupling map and native gates of a 127-qubit device, showing the accuracy of analytic resource estimates to be strongly algorithm dependent. The implementation is validated with 119 automated tests at 96% code coverage and demonstrated through integration with an autonomous agent platform.

Abstract: Refactoring is essential for maintaining and evolving software systems, yet we still have limited insight into how automated code-generation agents describe these changes in pull requests. In this study, we analyze refactoring-related pull requests produced by five AI coding agents, with a particular focus on how their intentions are communicated through pull request descriptions. To better understand recurring transformation patterns, we extract refactoring descriptors terms that capture different refactoring activities and use them to identify similarities across agents.
